concept.name: Long-legged doji
concept.definition: A doji variant with long upper and lower shadows and open and close at or near the same price, typically near the middle of the period's range. It is interpreted in technical analysis as strong two-sided pressure ending in a standoff, often read as a sign that the prior trend is losing conviction.
concept.intuition: Price was pushed far up and far down during the period, but neither side could hold its gains; the market ended exactly where it began after a wide-ranging battle.
concept.mechanics: Identified from OHLC data as a candle with a near-zero real body (open approximately equal to close) whose upper and lower shadows are both long relative to the body and typically to recent candles. No strict numerical threshold is canonical; charting packages apply their own body/range rules.
concept.failure_modes: It only shows indecision, not direction; in choppy or low-volume markets long-legged dojis are common and meaningless. Treating it as a standalone reversal signal produces frequent false positives.
concept.misconceptions: It is not inherently bearish or bullish; its meaning depends entirely on the preceding trend and on confirmation from subsequent candles.
concept.example: After a two-week uptrend, a stock opens at 100, trades between 95 and 105, and closes at 100.05. The long-legged doji marks exhaustion of both sides; traders watch the next session to see which way the stalemate resolves.
